title: Inside Karl-Anthony Towns’ Journey From Phenom to NBA Champ
text:
How Karl-Anthony Towns’ New Jersey Roots Helped the Knicks Win a Championship Search sneakers, brands, or styles... Sign In SHOP STYLE SNEAKERS MUSIC SPORTS POP CULTURE BETS COVER STORIES VERZUZ WATCH COMMUNITY Bets How Karl-Anthony Towns’ New Jersey Roots Helped the Knicks Win a Championship
 Karl-Anthony Towns went from a local phenom to NBA champion. Now, on his 31st birthday, KAT’s high school teammates recount how it all started. 
 By Sameer Kumar November 15, 2026 Comments Comment Save Share Comments Comments Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images Karl-Anthony Towns was a freshman at St. Joseph High School in Metuchen, N.J., when he accepted that he might not be his team’s go-to guy every night.
 The Falcons were led by senior Quenton DeCosey, a rim-attacking forward considered the team’s best player.
 Towns, nearly seven feet tall with the skills of a guard, could’ve demanded infinite scoring opportunities. Instead, he learned to play the high post, where his shooting pulled defenders away from the rim and his passing turned DeCosey’s drives into easier looks.

 “Karl really came in and understood, like, ‘Hey, I might not be the guy some nights,’” former St. Joe’s guard Jimbo Long tells Complex. “So he took it into his hands, making great passes, like you were seeing the NBA Finals playing off the high post.”
 More than a decade later, some of the lessons Towns learned from his New Jersey upbringing—teamwork, selflessness, sacrifice, and versatility—helped the New York Knicks win a championship alongside Jalen Brunson , OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart.
 Towns’ role during New York’s title run resembled his responsibilities at St. Joe’s. After falling 2-1 to the Atlanta Hawks in the first round, Knicks head coach Mike Brown increasingly used Towns at the high post, creating more opportunities for him to drive and facilitate. As a result, New York’s offense found another dimension. The Knicks lost just once more that postseason: Game 3 of the NBA Finals against the San Antonio Spurs .
 Towns was just as engaged on defense, absorbing blow after blow from Victor Wembanyama and often keeping him out of the paint. In Game 4, after Anunoby’s momentous tip-in gave New York a narrow 107-106 lead, Towns deflected San Antonio’s final inbounds pass, helping seal the Knicks’ historic 29-point comeback victory.
 Towns’ recognition that sacrificing individual stats can have an immediate impact on winning dates back to his high school days. The Falcons went 29-2 and finished fifth in the state in his first season at St. Joe’s. Perhaps not so coincidentally, the Knicks won a championship in Towns' second season in New York.
 From St. Joe’s to the University of Kentucky 
 Well before making the NBA, Towns had attributes that clearly set him apart from other hoopers his age. He developed them with his father, Karl Towns Sr., a former forward at Monmouth University who also coached the men’s team at Piscataway Vo-Tech.
 During one workout, Towns Sr. intentionally fired difficult passes from beneath the basket. Karl-Anthony caught each one, squared up, and drained 10 consecutive 3-pointers from 10 different spots without a single shot touching the rim.
 “You’re gonna have to change your phone number,” Jerry Carino of the Asbury Park Press recalls telling Towns Sr. following the workout.
 Big men were traditionally expected to inflict their damage near the basket. Former Los Angeles Lakers center and fellow St. Joe’s alum Andrew Bynum was infamously benched for attempting a 3-pointer in the middle of a game.
 Much to the chagrin of many players and coaches from around the area, then-St. Joe’s coach Dave Turco encouraged Towns to keep letting it fly, and his signature stepback became the most talked-about part of his game.
 “Who am I to say that he shouldn't be shooting 3s?” former St. Joe’s forward James Ziemba said. “When he stepped on the court, he was probably the best shooter on the court for his entire high school career.”
 Before arriving at St. Joe’s, Towns joined AAU program Sports U - Team IZOD. Towns was the only player in program history allowed to play up an age group, competing against 15-year-olds at just 14, and he stayed with the program until he packed his bags for the University of Kentucky .
 “We wanted to produce a certain type of scholar-athlete,” coach Eddie Bright Jr. tells Complex. “We wanted kids that would be successful when that ball stopped bouncing. We wanted kids who would grow up to be great husbands, fathers, citizens, and leaders.”
 Towns also had a plan for life off the court. He strived to enter the medical field before starting high school and prepared a list of courses to take at St. Joe’s. When he needed assistance with his college application essay, he asked World Literature teacher Chris Harring. Towns then studied kinesiology in his lone year enrolled at Kentucky.
 “He always chose to have his stuff in order in the classroom because that's just who he was,” Harring said. “He was the kind of person who wanted to make sure everything he did was at the highest level possible because he always wanted to represent himself, his family, and what he was taught well to the highest degree.”
 For a kid with Towns's potential, the path to basketball stardom could have taken him far from home, to a national sports academy or another high-profile program. Instead, he stayed close to Piscataway.
 “He didn't change high schools like socks,” Jerry Carino says. “I think the constant jumping of high schools really hurts a teenager's personal development.
 “He had a real high school experience for three years. I think that all really contributed to him becoming super coachable, a great teammate, and a really well-adjusted human being.”
 Following his freshman year at St. Joe’s, Towns represented the Dominican Republic at the 2012 FIBA Olympic Qualifying Tournament, playing under John Calipari , his future coach at Kentucky.
 Despite being born in Edison, N.J., Towns chose to represent his mother’s native country, falling in love with the D.R. after visiting the nation when he was 15 years old.
 From that experience, he gained noticeable strength and added more dunks, hook shots and fadeaways to his repertoire.
 “That's when he really solidified himself as the best player in the state,” Long said. “That’s when he became unstoppable.”
 Towns generated so much buzz that big-name coaches, such as Tom Izzo, Jay Wright and Calipari, started making the trek to Metuchen, and an MSG Varsity camera crew filmed a documentary about Towns during his sophomore year of high school.
 Future NBA first-round pick Wade Baldwin IV and Marques Townes, who was a key part of No. 11 Loyola-Chicago’s run to the 2018 Final Four, transferred to St. Joe's explicitly to team up with Towns. In their second season as teammates, the trio led the Falcons to the 2014 NJSIAA Tournament of Champions title.
 Starring alongside highly recruited prospects gave Towns an early lesson in sharing the floor with elite talent. At Kentucky, he joined forces with Devin Booker, Willie Cauley-Stein, and twins Aaron and Andrew Harrison, helping the Wildcats post an otherworldly 38-1 record before falling to Wisconsin in the Final Four.
 Before Towns joined the Knicks, he had a memorable nine-year run with the Minnesota Timberwolves after being drafted No. 1 overall in 2015, helping the franchise reach the Western Conference Finals for the first time in 20 years.
 He learned to share the spotlight with Anthony Edwards and Rudy Gobert, shifting to power forward to accommodate Gobert’s presence as a defensive anchor and interior scorer, a role he knew from playing next to Cauley-Stein at Kentucky.
 Prior to Minnesota’s ascent, the T-Wolves went through a lot of losing. Towns was also facing intense criticism and a “soft” label following his highly publicized fallout with Jimmy Butler, and his defensive positioning and decision-making sometimes drew scrutiny.
 Despite weathering plenty of cold storms in Minnesota, Towns never publicly called out his teammates or quit on his team. In fact, he was the first person to welcome his new head coach, Chris Finch, when he took over midway through the 2020-21 season.
 “He didn't have to call me and welcome me, and be super coachable,” Finch tells Complex “He could have just made me prove it to him, but he was probably the guy who welcomed me the most and did whatever we asked him to do.”
 Finch also remembers Towns looking after the coaching staff on road trips. Getting food on the plane was usually a rookie’s job, but Towns always made sure everybody was attended to.
 Family Values
 Towns was raised in a close-knit family, with his parents and his sister, Lachelle, instilling values of respect and kindness. No one has been more central to who he is than his mother.
 Throughout the Knicks’ run, Towns paid tribute to Jacqueline Cruz-Towns, who died in April 2020 of complications from COVID-19. He looked up to the sky in prayer, described feeling a calming presence from above, credited her with helping the Knicks get a game-clinching stop against Wembanyama in Game 2 of the Finals, and ultimately thanked her for guiding him through the title.
 “After that miss for San Antonio, I was just in tears at home,” Carino shared. “Because he loves his mother. He's got his father's basketball ability but his mother’s personality. His mother was just a wonderful, fun-loving human being.”
 While Towns might seem to have gone Hollywood since leaving the Garden State, he hosted A-list guests such as Timothée Chalamet, Kylie Jenner, and Michael B. Jordan at his fairy-tale wedding to Jordyn Woods, which reportedly cost $10 million. The people who knew him from Piscataway say otherwise.
 Carino recalled that Towns bought ice cream for everyone at a local shop during the Knicks’ championship run, taking time to chat and pose for pictures with fans.
 Months before Towns helped bring championship glory back to New York, Ziemba had a chance to catch up with his old buddy right after Towns was done warming up before the Knicks took on the Phoenix Suns. Ziemba had congratulated Towns on his recent engagement to Woods.
 “He's not all of a sudden too big leagues to talk to his buddies from high school,” Ziemba said. “The success that he's had hasn't changed who he is as a person.”
 The same values Towns learned just a short drive outside of New York City helped him lift the Knicks to their first championship in 53 years. The people who watched him grow up are proud to see him stay true to himself while representing Middlesex County.
 “He's a champion now,” Ziemba says. “Karl’s vindicated. It vindicates who he is as a person, the way he carries himself, the way he is as a teammate.”
 Chris Harring, Towns’ former teacher, adds, “I said to my son, ‘You be a fan of Karl Towns, you're going to be a fan of the person that will be that ideal role model.’ There's no better role model to set your sights on, not just a basketball player, but a citizen of the world.”
